lesson.title: en: Of It
lesson.subtitle: en replaces de + noun and partitives: Tu veux du café ? — Oui, j'en veux.

hook.title: en: The Pronoun for 'Some', 'Any', and 'Of Them'
hook.content: Whenever you replace a partitive quantity (du pain, de la soupe, de l'eau, des amis) or a noun after a number/amount (un, deux, un peu de), put en (/ɑ̃/) right before the verb: J'en veux ('I want some'), J'en ai deux ('I have two of them')!

footnotes.title: Why 'J'en ai un' keeps 'un' at the back while 'en' walks to the front
footnotes.content: When you drop the noun after a number ('I have one [coffee]'), the 'of it' (en) walks left of the verb while the number 'one' (un) stays at the end: J'en ai un!

pattern.title: Replace de/du/de la/des + Noun with en Before the Verb
pattern.content: Keep any number or quantity word at the end and place en before the verb.
pattern.linguist_note: Partitive clitic en (< Latin inde) is obligatory whenever a quantified noun phrase is pronominalized.
pattern.trap_note: Never say *J'ai deux when answering 'Do you have brothers?' — always include en: J'en ai deux!

exercises.prompt: Match each question with its natural en response:

matching_pairs.german: Oui, j'en veux (Yes, I want some)
Oui, j'en prends un peu (I'll have a little of it)

matching_pairs.english: Tu as des sœurs ? (two of them)
matching_pairs.german: Oui, j'en ai deux (Yes, I have two of them)

matching_pairs.english: Tu as un billet ? (one of them)
matching_pairs.german: Oui, j'en ai un (Yes, I have one)
Non, je n'en veux pas (No, I don't want any)

exercises.target_answer: Oui, j'en veux (Yes, I want some), Oui, j'en prends un peu (I'll have a little of it), Oui, j'en ai deux (Yes, I have two of them), Oui, j'en ai un (Yes, I have one), Non, je n'en veux pas (No, I don't want any)
exercises.meaning: Tu veux du fromage ? (some cheese), Tu prends du café ? (a little), Tu as des sœurs ? (two of them), Tu as un billet ? (one of them), Tu veux du vin ? (none)
exercises.explanation: en replaces the noun while numbers and un peu stay after the verb.

exercises.prompt: What is the literal word-for-word structure of 'J'en veux un peu'?
exercises.natural: I want a little of it
options: I want a little of it
exercises.meaning: Literal structure: I of-it want a little
exercises.explanation: en ('of-it') walks before veux, leaving un peu at the end.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks 'Vous avez des frères ?' ('Do you have brothers?'). How do you answer 'Yes, I have three'?
exercises.explanation: When a number stands without its noun, en is mandatory before the verb: J'en ai trois!

exercises.idea: yes I want two of them (using Oui, j'en veux deux)
cues: Yes, I of-them want two → Oui, j'en veux deux
idea_parts: subject + en + verb + number → j'en veux deux
exercises.meaning: Yes, I want two of them
exercises.explanation: en walks before veux while deux stays after.

diagnosis.cue: Include en before veux: Oui, j'en veux deux.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Je n'en ai pas besoin aujourd'hui
exercises.target_answer: Je n'en ai pas besoin aujourd'hui
exercises.explanation: avoir besoin DE quelque chose takes en ('of it'): Je n'en ai pas besoin!
exercises.affirmation: You spotted that avoir besoin de uses en!

summary.outcome: Use en before the verb to replace partitives, de-phrases, and nouns after numbers/quantities.

use_example.german: Tu as du pain ? — Oui, j'en ai beaucoup.
use_example.english: Do you have bread? — Yes, I have a lot of it.

summary.takeaway: Whenever a number or quantity stands without its noun, en must stand before the verb (J'en ai deux).

twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Oui, j'en veux deux" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of en: Of It.

en_pron.english_meaning: of it, of them, some, any
en_pron.context_phrase: Tu veux du café ? — Oui, j'en veux.
en_pron.context_translation: Do you want coffee? — Yes, I want some (of it).
en_pron.etymology_derivation: Whenever a verb or quantity uses de/du/de la/des, en replaces the whole phrase and walks left of the verb!

vouloir.etymology_derivation: Latin volō 'I want' → vouloir. A volunteer is the one who wants to do — the want-root English kept in voluntary, benevolent.

avoir.etymology_derivation: Latin habēre = have. The H dropped and stayed dropped — French never pronounces its Latin H.

pain.etymology_derivation: Latin pānis 'bread' — a pantry is literally the bread-room. The N is thought, not said: the nasal vowel is the lesson.

café.etymology_derivation: Turkish kahve → Italian caffè → French café. English took the same journey twice: coffee and café.

eau.shift_rule: Latin aqua, all three vowels are ghosts of a
eau.etymology_derivation: Latin aqua → ea → eau: one syllable wearing two vowels and a consonant as historical scar tissue. Feminine: l'eau.

deux.etymology_derivation: Latin duo — English duo, deuce (the two-card).

un_peu.etymology_derivation: Latin paucus 'a small amount' gave English 'paucity' and French peu — one root, two registers.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
